claim: The nucleosome is the atomic unit of chromatin.
source: The nucleosome is the atomic unit of chromatin.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about chromatin structure.

claim: Nucleosomes passively and actively template the majority of nuclear interactions essential to life by determining target site access for transcription factors.
source: Nucleosomes passively and actively template the majority of nuclear interactions essential to life by determining target site access for transcription factors (Spitz and Furlong, 2012), bookmarking active and repressed chromosomal compartments via post-translational modifications (Zhou et al., 2011), and safeguarding the genome from mutational agents (Papamichos-Chronakis and Peterson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spitz and Furlong, 2012.

claim: Nucleosomes bookmark active and repressed chromosomal compartments via post-translational modifications.
source: Nucleosomes passively and actively template the majority of nuclear interactions essential to life by determining target site access for transcription factors (Spitz and Furlong, 2012), bookmarking active and repressed chromosomal compartments via post-translational modifications (Zhou et al., 2011), and safeguarding the genome from mutational agents (Papamichos-Chronakis and Peterson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: Nucleosomes safeguard the genome from mutational agents.
source: Nucleosomes passively and actively template the majority of nuclear interactions essential to life by determining target site access for transcription factors (Spitz and Furlong, 2012), bookmarking active and repressed chromosomal compartments via post-translational modifications (Zhou et al., 2011), and safeguarding the genome from mutational agents (Papamichos-Chronakis and Peterson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Papamichos-Chronakis and Peterson, 2013.

claim: The earliest views of the beads-on-a-string arrangement of chromatin derived from classical electron micrographs of chromatin fibres.
source: Our earliest views of the beads-on-a-string arrangement of chromatin derived from classical electron micrographs of chromatin fibres (Olins and Olins, 1974), which have since been followed by both light (Huang et al., 2010) and electron microscopy (Ou et al., 2017; Song et al., 2014) studies of in vitro-assembled and in vivo chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Olins and Olins, 1974.

claim: SAMOSA combines adenine methyltransferase footprinting and single-molecule real-time DNA sequencing to natively and nondestructively measure nucleosome positions on individual chromatin fibres.
source: SAMOSA is a high-throughput single-molecule sequencing method that combines adenine methyltransferase footprinting and single-molecule real-time DNA sequencing to natively and nondestructively measure nucleosome positions on individual chromatin fibres.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in this study.

claim: SAMOSA data allows unbiased classification of single-molecular 'states' of nucleosome occupancy on individual chromatin fibres.
source: SAMOSA data allows unbiased classification of single-molecular 'states' of nucleosome occupancy on individual chromatin fibres.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chromatin is comprised of both regular and irregular single-molecular oligonucleosome patterns that differ subtly in their relative abundance across epigenomic domains.
source: Our analyses suggest that chromatin is comprised of both regular and irregular single-molecular oligonucleosome patterns that differ subtly in their relative abundance across epigenomic domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering and epigenomic domain analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Irregularity in oligonucleosome patterns is particularly striking in constitutive heterochromatin.
source: This irregularity is particularly striking in constitutive heterochromatin, which has typically been viewed as a conformationally static entity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analyses of H3K9me3 and satellite DNA presented in the manuscript.

claim: High-accuracy PacBio single-molecule real-time sequencing can detect m6dA deposited on chromatin templates to natively measure nucleosome positioning.
source: We hypothesized that high-accuracy PacBio single-molecule real-time sequencing could detect m6dA deposited on chromatin templates to natively measure nucleosome positioning.
evidence: This hypothesis is tested and supported by the in vitro validation experiments.

claim: Nonanucleosomal chromatin arrays were generated through salt-gradient dialysis using template DNA containing nine tandem repetitive copies of the Widom 601 nucleosome positioning sequence separated by ~46 basepairs of linker sequence.
source: To test this hypothesis, we used the nonspecific adenine methyltransferase EcoGII (Murray et al., 2018) to footprint nonanucleosomal chromatin arrays generated through salt-gradient dialysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), using template DNA containing nine tandem repetitive copies of the Widom 601 nucleosome positioning sequence (Lowary and Widom, 1998) separated by ~46 basepairs (bp) of linker sequence followed by ~450 bp of sequence without any known intrinsic affinity for nucleosomes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for in vitro validation.

claim: A total of 33,594 single molecules were analyzed across all three in vitro conditions.
source: After filtering low quality reads, we analyzed a total of 33,594 single molecules across all three conditions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of molecules analyzed.

claim: Higher average interpulse duration (IPD) was observed in samples exposed to methyltransferase, consistent with a rolling circle polymerase 'pausing' at methylated adenine residues in template DNA.
source: Across both platforms, we observed higher average interpulse duration (IPD) in samples exposed to methyltransferase, consistent with a rolling circle polymerase 'pausing' at methylated adenine residues in template DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Footprinted chromatin samples sequenced on either platform revealed strong specificity for altered IPD values only at thymines falling outside Widom 601 repeat sequences.
source: Further inspection of footprinted chromatin samples sequenced on either platform revealed strong specificity for altered IPD values only at thymines falling outside Widom 601 repeat sequences, in contrast with fully methylated naked template and unmethylated controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Modification patterns were subtly influenced by the associated 10-mer context of sequenced bases, consistent with possible enzymatic biases and previous observations of sequence-influenced shifts in polymerase kinetics.
source: These patterns were subtly influenced by the associated 10-mer context of sequenced bases, consistent with possible enzymatic biases, but also previous observations of sequence-influenced shifts in polymerase kinetics (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Feng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and a citation to Feng et al., 2013.

claim: The PacBio platform can natively detect ectopic m6dA added to chromatinized templates.
source: These results suggest that the PacBio platform can natively detect ectopic m6dA added to chromatinized templates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro validation experiments.

claim: SAMOSA data can be used to accurately infer nucleosome dyad positions given a strong positioning sequence.
source: SAMOSA data can be used to accurately infer nucleosome dyad positions given a strong positioning sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1B showing the distribution of called dyad positions.

claim: Called dyads fall within a few nucleotides of the expected dyad position (median ±median absolute deviation [MAD]=4 ± 2.97 bp).
source: Observed dyads were highly concordant with expected positions (median ±median absolute deviation [MAD]=4 ± 2.97 bp), consistent with our data accurately capturing the expected 601 dyad.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the dyad calling analysis.

claim: SAMOSA data accurately recapitulates the known nucleosome repeat lengths (NRL) of in vitro assembled chromatin fibres.
source: SAMOSA data accurately recapitulates the known nucleosome repeat lengths (NRL) of in vitro assembled chromatin fibres.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1C showing NRL measurements.

claim: Called NRLs are strongly concordant with the expected 193 repeat length (pairwise distance between adjacent dyads median ±MAD = 193±7.40 bp; single-molecule averaged repeat length median ±MAD = 192±1.30 bp).
source: Compared with the expected repeat length of 193 bp, our calculated results were similarly accurate at both two-dyad resolution (pairwise distance between adjacent dyads; median ±MAD = 193±7.40 bp) and averaged single-molecule resolution (median ±MAD = 192±1.30 bp).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the NRL analysis.

claim: Modification patterns occurred in expected linker sequences and not in unmethylated or fully methylated control samples.
source: Finally, we directly visualized the modification probabilities of individual sequenced chromatin molecules and observed that modification patterns occurred in expected linker sequences (Figure 1D), and not in unmethylated or fully methylated control samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 6A,B.

claim: EcoGII footprinting is specific for unprotected DNA.
source: These results demonstrate that EcoGII footprinting is specific for unprotected DNA and that kinetic deviations observed in the data are not simply the result of primary sequence biases in the template itself.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro validation experiments.

claim: A light micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digest followed by disruption of the nuclear envelope and overnight dialysis can be used to gently liberate oligonucleosomes into solution without dramatically perturbing nucleosomal structure.
source: Multiple prior studies have suggested that a light micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digest followed by disruption of the nuclear envelope and overnight dialysis can be used to gently liberate oligonucleosomes into solution without dramatically perturbing nucleosomal structure (Ehrensberger et al., 2015; Gilbert and Allan, 2001; Gilbert et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ehrensberger et al., 2015; Gilbert and Allan, 2001; Gilbert et al., 2004.

claim: A total of 1,855,316 molecules were sequenced from K562 oligonucleosomes on the Sequel II platform.
source: After lightly digesting and solubilizing oligonucleosomes from human K562 nuclei, we methylated chromatin with EcoGII and sequenced methylated molecules on the Sequel II platform (n = 1,855,316 molecules total; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of molecules sequenced.

claim: In vivo SAMOSA combines MNase-derived cuts flanking each fragment with methyltransferase footprinting of nucleosomes.
source: Our approach combines MNase-derived cuts flanking each fragment with methyltransferase footprinting of nucleosomes.
evidence: This describes the dual-omic nature of the in vivo SAMOSA method.

claim: MNase cuts mark the boundary of genomic 'barrier' elements like nucleosomes and can be tuned by modifying digestion conditions.
source: MNase cuts mark the boundary of genomic 'barrier' elements like nucleosomes and can be tuned by modifying digestion conditions; accordingly, fragment length distributions from in vivo SAMOSA data display patterns emblematic of bulk nucleosomal array regularity (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fragment length distributions from in vivo SAMOSA data display patterns emblematic of bulk nucleosomal array regularity.
source: MNase cuts mark the boundary of genomic 'barrier' elements like nucleosomes and can be tuned by modifying digestion conditions; accordingly, fragment length distributions from in vivo SAMOSA data display patterns emblematic of bulk nucleosomal array regularity (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Modification patterns of sequenced molecules capture nucleosome-positioning information at single-molecule resolution.
source: Modification patterns of sequenced molecules then capture nucleosome-positioning information at single-molecule resolution; this is evident in single-molecule averages of modification probability in chromatin samples with respect to fully methylated and unmethylated controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SAMOSA is the first method that simultaneously captures the positioning of protein-DNA interactions through nucleolytic cleavage and the positioning of proximal protein-DNA interactions through DNA methylation on the same single-molecule.
source: While previous approaches for studying nucleosome regularity may capture each of the former information types, this method is, to our knowledge, the first that simultaneously captures the positioning of protein-DNA interactions through nucleolytic cleavage, and (through DNA methylation) the positioning of proximal protein-DNA interactions on the same single-molecule.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the method.

claim: SAMOSA data can be paired with a state-of-the-art community detection algorithm to systematically cluster footprinted molecules on the basis of single-molecule nucleosome regularity and NRL.
source: Given the single-molecule nature of SAMOSA, we speculated that our data could be paired with a state-of-the-art community detection algorithm to systematically cluster footprinted molecules on the basis of single-molecule nucleosome regularity and NRL (i.e. 'oligonucleosome patterns').
evidence: This describes the clustering approach used in the study.

claim: Unsupervised Leiden clustering of autocorrelograms resulted in seven clusters.
source: To ease detection of signal regularity on single molecules, we computed autocorrelograms for each molecule in our dataset ≥500 bp in length, and subjected resulting values to unsupervised Leiden clustering (Traag et al., 2019). Cluster sizes varied considerably, but were consistent across both replicates, with each cluster containing 6.54% (Cluster 4)–20.1% (Cluster 1) of all molecules (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis and Figure 3A.

claim: The seven clusters capture the spectrum of oligonucleosome patterning genome-wide, stratifying the genome by both NRL and array regularity.
source: The resulting seven clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) capture the spectrum of oligonucleosome patterning genome-wide, stratifying the genome by both NRL and array regularity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering results.

claim: SAMOSA data broadly fall into two categories: irregular clusters made up of molecules spanning multiple NRLs and lacking a strong regular periodicity, and highly regular clusters with defined single-molecule NRLs ranging from ~172 bp to >200 bp.
source: Our data broadly fall into two categories: irregular clusters made up of molecules spanning multiple NRLs and lacking a strong regular periodicity, and highly regular clusters with defined single-molecule NRLs ranging from ~172 bp (i.e. chromatosome plus 5 bp DNA) to >200 bp.
evidence: This is a summary of the clustering results.

claim: SAMOSA captures the transient nucleosome occupancy of transcription-factor-binding motifs.
source: SAMOSA captures the transient nucleosome occupancy of transcription-factor-binding motifs
evidence: This is supported by the transcription factor binding site analyses.

claim: Inspection of cleavage patterns about six different TF-binding sites (CTCF, NRF1, NRSF/REST, PU.1, c-MYC, GATA1) revealed signal resembling traditional MNase-seq data, with fragment ends accumulating immediately proximal to predicted TF-binding motifs.
source: Inspection of cleavage patterns about six different TF-binding sites (CTCF, NRF1, NRSF/REST, PU.1, c-MYC, GATA1) (Figure 4A–F) revealed signal resembling traditional MNase-seq data, with fragment ends accumulating immediately proximal to predicted TF-binding motifs, and, in the case of some TFs (i.e. CTCF, REST, PU.1), showed characteristic patterns of phased nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–F.

claim: Some TFs (i.e. CTCF, REST, PU.1) showed characteristic patterns of phased nucleosomes.
source: Inspection of cleavage patterns about six different TF-binding sites (CTCF, NRF1, NRSF/REST, PU.1, c-MYC, GATA1) (Figure 4A–F) revealed signal resembling traditional MNase-seq data, with fragment ends accumulating immediately proximal to predicted TF-binding motifs, and, in the case of some TFs (i.e. CTCF, REST, PU.1), showed characteristic patterns of phased nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–F.

claim: Analysis of m6dA signal in sequenced molecules harboring motifs revealed examples of methyltransferase accessibility coincident with TF motifs (e.g. CTCF, NRF1, c-MYC).
source: Further analysis of m6dA signal in sequenced molecules harboring motifs with at least 500 nucleotides of flanking DNA revealed examples of methyltransferase accessibility coincident with TF motifs (e.g. CTCF, NRF1, c-MYC), but also cases where single-molecule averages demonstrated weak or no differential signal when compared to equal numbers of molecules drawn from random genomic regions matched for GC-percentage and repeat content (e.g. GATA1; Figure 4G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G–L.

claim: Some TF-binding sites (e.g. GATA1) showed weak or no differential m6dA signal when compared to control regions.
source: Further analysis of m6dA signal in sequenced molecules harboring motifs with at least 500 nucleotides of flanking DNA revealed examples of methyltransferase accessibility coincident with TF motifs (e.g. CTCF, NRF1, c-MYC), but also cases where single-molecule averages demonstrated weak or no differential signal when compared to equal numbers of molecules drawn from random genomic regions matched for GC-percentage and repeat content (e.g. GATA1; Figure 4G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G–L.

claim: SAMOSA methylation data do not appear to capture TF 'footprints' as seen in DNase I, hydroxyl radical, or MNase cleavage data.
source: Importantly, our methylation data do not appear to capture TF 'footprints' as seen in DNase I, hydroxyl radical, or MNase cleavage data—this could be due to turnover of transcription factors during our solubilization process, or owed to sterics, as EcoGII is roughly twice the molecular weight of S. aureus micrococcal nuclease (Murray et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with speculation about the cause.

claim: Leiden clustering of molecules containing TF-binding sites defined 13 discrete states of template accessibility.
source: To test whether our assay captured such signal, we clustered all molecules shown in Figure 4G–L (including control molecules) using Leiden clustering, using modification probabilities extracted in a 500 bp window surrounding the predicted motif site/control site. In total, we defined 13 discrete states of template accessibility across all surveyed molecules (Figure 4M; cluster sizes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis and Figure 4M.

claim: Most transcription factors (excepting PU.1 and GATA1) were significantly enriched for specific accessibility states.
source: Notably, the patterns within these clusters were evident at single-molecule resolution (Figure 4N). Most transcription factors (excepting PU.1 and GATA1—the latter of which may productively bind nucleosomal DNA [Zaret and Carroll, 2011]) were significantly enriched for specific states as defined above, and all control regions were markedly depleted for molecules harboring the accessible 'A' and 'HA' states, hinting at the biological relevance of these patterns (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: All control regions were markedly depleted for molecules harboring the accessible 'A' and 'HA' states.
source: Notably, the patterns within these clusters were evident at single-molecule resolution (Figure 4N). Most transcription factors (excepting PU.1 and GATA1—the latter of which may productively bind nucleosomal DNA [Zaret and Carroll, 2011]) were significantly enriched for specific states as defined above, and all control regions were markedly depleted for molecules harboring the accessible 'A' and 'HA' states, hinting at the biological relevance of these patterns (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Each epigenomic domain surveyed was comprised of a highly heterogeneous mixture of oligonucleosome patterns.
source: A striking finding of our analyses was that each epigenomic domain surveyed was comprised of a highly heterogeneous mixture of oligonucleosome patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: Oligonucleosome patterns differed only subtly from control molecules with respect to regularity and NRL in most cases.
source: In most cases, these patterns differed only subtly from control molecules with respect to regularity and NRL.
evidence: This is an observation from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: A shift of ~5 bp (180 bp vs. 185 bp) in estimated median NRLs was observed for H3K9me3 chromatin with respect to random molecules.
source: In specific cases, we observed small effect shifts in the estimated median NRLs for specific domains—for example, a shift of ~5 bp (180 bp vs. 185 bp) in H3K9me3 chromatin with respect to random molecules, and a shift of ~4 bp (182 bp vs 186 bp) for H3K36me3.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: A shift of ~4 bp (182 bp vs 186 bp) in estimated median NRLs was observed for H3K36me3 chromatin.
source: In specific cases, we observed small effect shifts in the estimated median NRLs for specific domains—for example, a shift of ~5 bp (180 bp vs. 185 bp) in H3K9me3 chromatin with respect to random molecules, and a shift of ~4 bp (182 bp vs 186 bp) for H3K36me3.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: H3K4me3 decorated chromatin had markedly fewer (78.0% vs 88.6%) successful peak calls compared to control molecules, consistent with the expected irregularity of active promoter oligonucleosomes.
source: These shifts were also evident in the fraction of molecules with successful peak calls: H3K4me3 decorated chromatin, for example, had markedly fewer (78.0% vs 88.6%) successful calls compared to control molecules, a finding consistent with the expected irregularity of active promoter oligonucleosomes.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: All measured parameters would be unattainable using any existing biochemical method.
source: We note that all these measured parameters would be unattainable using any existing biochemical method and that these preliminary findings argue against the abundance of homogeneous oligonucleosome structures in either heterochromatic or euchromatic nuclear regions.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and capabilities of the method.

claim: These preliminary findings argue against the abundance of homogeneous oligonucleosome structures in either heterochromatic or euchromatic nuclear regions.
source: We note that all these measured parameters would be unattainable using any existing biochemical method and that these preliminary findings argue against the abundance of homogeneous oligonucleosome structures in either heterochromatic or euchromatic nuclear regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: Chromatin domains are demarcated by their relative usage of specific oligonucleosome patterns.
source: One possible explanation for this is that epigenomic domains subtly, but significantly, vary in their relative composition of distinct oligonucleosome patterns, and the resulting average of these differences is the signal captured in MNase-Southern and other cleavage-based measurements. We tested this hypothesis by constructing a series of statistical tests to determine whether each of the seven defined oligonucleosome patterns were significantly enriched or depleted across chromatin domains and matched control regions (Figure 6C; reproducibility analyses summarized in Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Our results suggest that chromatin domains are demarcated by their relative usage of specific oligonucleosome patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by the enrichment analyses shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Active chromatin marked by H3K4me3 and H3K4me1 are punctuated by a mixture of irregular oligonucleosome patterns (namely, clusters IRL and IR170).
source: Consistent with expectations, active chromatin marked by H3K4me3 and H3K4me1 are punctuated by a mixture of irregular oligonucleosome patterns (namely, clusters IRL and IR170).
evidence: This is an observation from the enrichment analyses.

claim: H3K36me3-domains are punctuated by irregular IRS oligonucleosome patterns (Fisher's Exact Odds Ratio [O.R.]=1.13; q = 1.71E-50) and regular, short NRL172 patterns (O.R. = 1.39; q = 3.69E-170).
source: Our data partially corroborate this finding in human K562 cells: H3K36me3-domains are punctuated by irregular IRS oligoncleosome patterns (Fisher's Exact Odds Ratio [O.R.]=1.13; q = 1.71E-50) and regular, short NRL172 patterns (O.R. = 1.39; q = 3.69E-170).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the enrichment analyses.

claim: Across both H3K9me3 and Satellite molecules, enrichment for irregular IRS nucleosome conformers was observed (Satellite O.R. = 1.13; q = 5.71E-11; H3K9me3 O.R. = 1.35; q = 3.95E-23).
source: Our data partially disagree with prior estimates—across both H3K9me3 and Satellite molecules we observe enrichment for irregular IRS nucleosome conformers (Satellite O.R. = 1.13; q = 5.71E-11; H3K9me3 O.R. = 1.35; q = 3.95E-23).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the enrichment analyses.

claim: Enriched irregular conformers in H3K9me3 and Satellite were accompanied by enrichment for regular NRL172 oligonucleosome patterns (Satellite O.R. = 1.61; q = 5.25E-80; H3K9me3 O.R. = 1.23; q = 3.86E-6).
source: Still, these enriched conformers were accompanied by enrichment for regular NRL172 oligonucleosome patterns for both states (Satellite O.R. = 1.61; q = 5.25E-80; H3K9me3 O.R. = 1.23; q = 3.86E-6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the enrichment analyses.

claim: Prior NRL estimates by short-read sequencing may have been confounded by in vivo heterogeneity in nucleosome positions.
source: These analyses demonstrate that prior NRL estimates by short-read sequencing may have been confounded by in vivo heterogeneity in nucleosome positions, that heterochromatic nucleosome conformations can be both irregular and diverse, and finally, highlight the value of SAMOSA for accurately studying nucleosome structure in heterochromatin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the heterochromatin analyses.

claim: Heterochromatic nucleosome conformations can be both irregular and diverse.
source: These analyses demonstrate that prior NRL estimates by short-read sequencing may have been confounded by in vivo heterogeneity in nucleosome positions, that heterochromatic nucleosome conformations can be both irregular and diverse, and finally, highlight the value of SAMOSA for accurately studying nucleosome structure in heterochromatin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the heterochromatin analyses.

claim: Epigenomic domains are comprised of a diverse array of oligonucleosome patterns varying substantially in intrinsic regularity and average distance between regularly spaced nucleosomes.
source: Taken as a whole, our data suggest two fundamental properties of human epigenomic domains: first, epigenomic domains are comprised of a diverse array of oligonucleosome patterns varying substantially in intrinsic regularity and average distance between regularly spaced nucleosomes; second: epigenomic domains are demarcated by their usage of these oligonucleosome patterns.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: Epigenomic domains are demarcated by their usage of oligonucleosome patterns.
source: Taken as a whole, our data suggest two fundamental properties of human epigenomic domains: first, epigenomic domains are comprised of a diverse array of oligonucleosome patterns varying substantially in intrinsic regularity and average distance between regularly spaced nucleosomes; second: epigenomic domains are demarcated by their usage of these oligonucleosome patterns.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: All epigenomic states are characterized by a diverse mixture of oligonucleosomal conformers.
source: We find that all epigenomic states are characterized by a diverse mixture of oligonucleosomal conformers—many conformational states are neither significantly depleted nor enriched with respect to all molecules surveyed, further hinting at the diverse composition of chromatin domains genome-wide.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the epigenomic domain analyses.

claim: SAMOSA has multiple advantages over existing methyltransferase-based sequencing approaches: it avoids primary sequence biases associated with GpC/CpG methyltransferase footprinting methods.
source: Our approach has multiple advantages over existing methyltransferase-based sequencing approaches: first, by using a relatively nonspecific methyltransferase, we avoid the primary sequence biases associated with GpC/CpG methyltransferase footprinting methods; second, by natively detecting modifications using the single-molecule real-time sequencer, we reduce enzymatic sequence bias and avoid sample damage associated with sodium bisulphite conversion; finally, and most importantly, our approach unlocks the study of protein-DNA interactions at length-scales previously unallowed by Illumina sequencing.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the method.

claim: SAMOSA reduces enzymatic sequence bias and avoids sample damage associated with sodium bisulphite conversion by natively detecting modifications.
source: Our approach has multiple advantages over existing methyltransferase-based sequencing approaches: first, by using a relatively nonspecific methyltransferase, we avoid the primary sequence biases associated with GpC/CpG methyltransferase footprinting methods; second, by natively detecting modifications using the single-molecule real-time sequencer, we reduce enzymatic sequence bias and avoid sample damage associated with sodium bisulphite conversion; finally, and most importantly, our approach unlocks the study of protein-DNA interactions at length-scales previously unallowed by Illumina sequencing.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the method.

claim: SAMOSA unlocks the study of protein-DNA interactions at length-scales previously unallowed by Illumina sequencing.
source: Our approach has multiple advantages over existing methyltransferase-based sequencing approaches: first, by using a relatively nonspecific methyltransferase, we avoid the primary sequence biases associated with GpC/CpG methyltransferase footprinting methods; second, by natively detecting modifications using the single-molecule real-time sequencer, we reduce enzymatic sequence bias and avoid sample damage associated with sodium bisulphite conversion; finally, and most importantly, our approach unlocks the study of protein-DNA interactions at length-scales previously unallowed by Illumina sequencing.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the method.

claim: The current SAMOSA protocol enriches fragments ranging from ~500 bp to ~ 2 kb in size.
source: While the current SAMOSA protocol enriches fragments ranging from ~500 bp to ~ 2 kb in size, high-quality PacBio CCS sequencing is compatible with fragments ranging from 10 to 15 kbp.
evidence: This is a description of the current protocol's capabilities.

claim: High-quality PacBio CCS sequencing is compatible with fragments ranging from 10 to 15 kbp.
source: While the current SAMOSA protocol enriches fragments ranging from ~500 bp to ~ 2 kb in size, high-quality PacBio CCS sequencing is compatible with fragments ranging from 10 to 15 kbp.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of PacBio sequencing.

claim: With further optimization, SAMOSA will be applicable to longer arrays, enabling kilobase-domain-scale study of single-molecule oligonucleosome patterning.
source: We anticipate that with further optimization (e.g. optimization of digestion conditions), SAMOSA will be applicable to longer arrays, enabling kilobase-domain-scale study of single-molecule oligonucleosome patterning.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: SAMOSA is unlikely to capture protein-DNA interactions weaker or more transient than the stable nucleosome-DNA interaction because it involves methylating fibres following solubilization of oligonucleosomal fragments.
source: Second, our approach involves methylating fibres following solubilization of oligonucleosomal fragments, and is thus unlikely to capture protein-DNA interactions weaker or more transient than the stable nucleosome-DNA interaction.
evidence: This is a limitation of the current protocol.

claim: The proof-of-concept was performed in unsynchronized K562 cells, so the contribution of biological processes like the cell cycle to the observed heterogeneity cannot yet be addressed.
source: Third, our proof-of-concept was performed in unsynchronized K562 cells, and thus we cannot yet address the contribution of a biological process like the cell cycle to the observed heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a limitation of the current study.

claim: As a proof-of-concept, the approach falls short of generating a high-coverage reference map of the K562 epigenome.
source: Finally, as a proof-of-concept our approach falls short of generating a high-coverage reference map of the K562 epigenome; as sequencing costs for PacBio decrease and sequence-enrichment technologies (e.g. CRISPR-based enrichment Ebbert et al., 2018; SMRT-ChIP [Wu et al., 2016]) for the platform mature, SAMOSA may routinely be used to generate reference datasets with hundred-to-thousand-fold single-molecular coverage of genomic sites of interest.
evidence: This is a limitation of the current study.

claim: The human epigenome is made up of a diverse array of oligonucleosome patterns, including highly regular arrays of varying nucleosome repeat lengths, and irregular arrays where nucleosomes are positioned without a detectable periodic signature.
source: Our data confirms that the human epigenome is made up of a diverse array of oligonucleosome patterns, including highly regular arrays of varying nucleosome repeat lengths, and irregular arrays where nucleosomes are positioned without a detectable periodic signature (Baldi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: SAMOSA results broadly agree with a recent approach employing electron tomography to map the in situ structure of mammalian nuclei, which found chromatin to be highly heterogeneous at the length scale of multi-nucleosome interactions.
source: Our results broadly agree with a recent approach employing electron tomography to map the in situ structure of mammalian nuclei, which found chromatin to be highly heterogeneous at the length scale of multi-nucleosome interactions, and failed to detect evidence of a 30 nm fibre or other homogeneous higher order compaction states (Ou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to Ou et al., 2017.

claim: Both mappable (H3K9me3 ChIP-seq peaks) and unmappable (human satellite sequence) constitutive heterochromatin are enriched for irregular oligonucleosome patterns in addition to expected regular arrays.
source: Surprisingly, we find that both mappable (H3K9me3 ChIP-seq peaks) and unmappable (human satellite sequence) constitutive heterochromatin are enriched for irregular oligonucleosome patterns in addition to expected regular arrays—the presence of these irregular fibres may have been previously missed due to an understandable reliance on bulk averaged methods (e.g. MNase-Southern) for studying constitutive heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a key finding from the heterochromatin analyses.

claim: The presence of irregular fibres in heterochromatin may have been previously missed due to reliance on bulk averaged methods.
source: Surprisingly, we find that both mappable (H3K9me3 ChIP-seq peaks) and unmappable (human satellite sequence) constitutive heterochromatin are enriched for irregular oligonucleosome patterns in addition to expected regular arrays—the presence of these irregular fibres may have been previously missed due to an understandable reliance on bulk averaged methods (e.g. MNase-Southern) for studying constitutive heterochromatin.
evidence: This is an inference about why previous studies missed this finding.

claim: Orthogonal analysis of heterochromatin-spanning K562 reads generated using the Fiber-seq method also reveal that H3K9me3 domains are enriched for irregular chromatin fibres.
source: This is strongly supported by orthogonal analysis of heterochromatin-spanning K562 reads generated using the recently published, conceptually similar Fiber-seq method (Stergachis et al., 2020), which also reveal that H3K9me3 domains are enriched for irregular chromatin fibres (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reanalysis of Fiber-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The irregularity in heterochromatin may be linked to the dynamic restructuring of heterochromatic nucleosomes by factors like HP1, which may promote phase-separation of heterochromatin.
source: Given the robustness of this finding, it is tempting to speculate that this irregularity may be linked to the dynamic restructuring of heterochromatic nucleosomes by factors like HP1 (Sanulli et al., 2019), which may promote phase-separation of heterochromatin.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance of the findings.
